roles: Healthcare Facility Director (hyper-focused on patient safety, zero false alarms, noise control).
Infection Control Officer (ICRA) (demands containment tents, HEPA vacuums, negative air pressure).
Contractor Lead Fire Alarm PM (responsible for schedule, budget, and system functionality).
Field Lead Technician / Electrician (responsible for physical wire pulls, ladder placement, device replacement).
Local Fire Marshal / AHJ (demands uninterrupted life-safety coverage during construction).
inputs: Architectural floor plan of the healthcare wing showing patient rooms, nurses' stations, and fire barriers.

Comprehensive stakeholder map; includes mobile dust containment and phased zone cutovers.
Delivers a turn-key ILSM manual that the hospital safety committee approves without edits.

workshops.transfer: Before stepping foot on any occupied commercial, industrial, or healthcare site, complete the Pre-Walk Stakeholder Checklist and identify the site authority who controls work permits.

objectives: Decompose a multi-site technical integration project into a 4-level Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) with 100% rule compliance.
Define measurable Work Packages with distinct completion criteria, labor budgets, and responsible roles.
Standardize branch rollout packages to create a repeatable "cookie-cutter" operational template.
roles: Senior Project Manager (governs multi-site schedule, standardization, and branch reporting).
Field Lead Foreman (manages physical travel, rough-in, device mounting, and branch technicians).
Systems Integration Programmer (handles NVR pre-staging, IP addressing, VMS cloud enrollment, reader programming).
inputs: Branch archetype floor plan (standard retail banking layout: teller line, vault, ATM lobby, manager office, drive-through).
Scope overview document detailing hardware quantities and milestone deadlines.
tasks: Build a graphical or indented 4-level WBS covering all phases (Central Engineering/Staging -> Branch Deployment -> Branch Commissioning -> Program Closeout).
Create a WBS Dictionary entry for two critical work packages: WP 2.3: Branch Staged Pre-Configuration and WP 3.4: Branch Physical Cutover & Acceptance.
Define the exact "Done" criteria for a branch to prevent technicians from leaving unfinished punch items behind.

mistakes: Structuring the WBS by physical trade tasks only, ignoring central procurement, staging, and administrative closeout. Debrief: Show that staging in the shop saves 60% of field travel time.
Vague work package definitions (e.g., "Install Cameras" instead of "Mount, Terminate, Aim, Focus, and Capture Acceptance Snapshot"). Debrief: Vague definitions lead to infinite punch lists.
Neglecting multi-site mobilization logistics (drive time, per diem, vehicle maintenance). Debrief: Factor travel and logistics directly into the WBS as distinct work packages.

rubric.desc: Merely lists hardware components without chronological or logical work packages.
Captures physical site work but misses pre-staging, travel logistics, and client IT coordination.
Well-structured 4-level WBS with clear work packages, dictionary definitions, and measurable completion gates.
Produces a highly optimized, modular "cookie-cutter" WBS where any technician can execute an identical branch deployment without supervision.

workshops.transfer: Never start a multi-location job without a standardized WBS template that includes Shop Staging, Field Deployment, and Client Sign-Off gates.

variations.small: Consolidate WBS to 3 levels; combine staging and procurement into a single lead technician package.
variations.large: Assign dedicated package owners (Central Staging Engineer vs. Mobile Field Foreman).

## WORKSHOP 5: COST ESTIMATING, MARGIN PROTECTION & CONTINGENCY IN A FIXED-PRICE NETWORK REFRESH BID
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 2 — Planning
- **Business Line:** Enterprise IT Services & LAN/WAN Refresh
- **Realistic Scenario:** A private academy with 3 buildings (Administration, High School, Athletics Center) requests a lump-sum fixed-price proposal to replace their aging network infrastructure: 14 Cisco Catalyst 9300 PoE switches, 3 core switches, 60 Cat6A patch cables, 4 UPS battery backups (APC 3000VA), and 1,200 feet of single-mode fiber optic backbone linking the buildings via existing underground exterior conduits.
  - *The Trap:* The RFP states that the winning contractor must guarantee that existing underground conduits are clear and usable; if blocked, the contractor is responsible for clearing or re-routing at their own expense. 
  - *Company Baseline:* Target gross profit margin is 35%. Technician burdened cost is $52/hr; billing rate is $110/hr.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Calculate true Fully Burdened Labor Rates including vehicle, insurance, overhead, and non-productive tool time.
  2. Structure an accurate, multi-category Cost Estimate (Materials, Labor, Rentals, Subcontractors, Permits, Travel).
  3. Apply structured Risk Contingency and clear Exclusionary Assumptions to protect project gross margin against catastrophic underground unknowns.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 2 (WBS, Schedule & Cost Planning).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 105 Minutes (20m Burdened Cost & Margin Mechanics, 45m Estimating Worksheet Calculation, 25m Bid Presentation & Defense, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Senior Estimator / PM* (builds the numbers, defends labor hours and materials markup).
  - *Role B: Company Owner* (scrutinizes the gross margin percentage and cash flow outlay).
  - *Role C: School Business Manager (Client)* (pushes for the lowest price, tries to shift all conduit risk to bidder).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Campus site layout showing distances between buildings and exterior manholes.
  - Equipment wholesale pricing sheet with distributor tier discounts.
  - Contractor fully burdened labor cost worksheet.
- **The Task:**
  1. Calculate total project cost across all categories (Hardware, Direct Labor, Rentals, Travel).
  2. Evaluate the underground conduit clause: Calculate the financial impact if Conduit 2 is crushed or silted full.
  3. Price the project to achieve exactly a 35% gross profit margin while adding an explicit Risk Contingency.
  4. Write the mandatory proposal qualification clause regarding underground pathway integrity.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Completed Project Cost Estimating & Margin Worksheet, Risk-Adjusted Bid Letter with Qualifying Assumptions.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "Look at the clause: 'Contractor guarantees underground conduits are clear.' If you sign that contract and your fish tape hits a collapsed pipe under the asphalt roadway, how much does directional boring cost per foot? What happens to your 35% margin?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* Distinguish between *Markup* and *Margin*. (To get a 35% margin, you do not multiply cost by 1.35; you divide cost by 0.65!).
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Confusing Markup with Margin, resulting in a 10% lower profit than intended. *Debrief:* Drill the math: $10,000 cost / (1 - 0.35) = $15,385 selling price, NOT $13,500.
  2. *Mistake:* Accepting unlimited civil or structural risks (e.g., underground conduits, asbestos, ceiling plenum structural collapse). *Debrief:* Show the exact wording for pathway exclusions: *"Existing underground conduits assumed clean, dry, and with pull-string in place. Jetting, clearing, or trenching subject to T&M change order."*
  3. *Mistake:* Forgetting disposal, lift transport, and permit fees in the cost sheet. *Debrief:* Review standard "hidden job costs" checklist.
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Miscalculates margin; accepts underground conduit risk without contingency or exclusion.
  - *2 (Developing):* Calculates margin correctly but fails to add structured risk contingency for fiber termination testing.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Flawless cost estimate; achieves 35% target margin; attaches clear, professional qualification clauses.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Offers an alternate bid with a pre-bid camera inspection of the conduit to de-risk the job and outmaneuver competitors.

- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Focus heavily on the cash required to front $65,000 in Cisco hardware before the first milestone billing.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Separate pre-sales engineering hours from field labor installation hours.

### 3. DETAILED MILESTONE EXECUTION BREAKDOWN

#### MILESTONE 1: INITIATION, SITE SURVEY & SCOPE BASELINE
- **The Challenge:** Teams receive the original 6-page RFP and architectural blueprints. The client includes ambiguous phrases: *"Contractor responsible for complete operational readiness across all facilities."*
- **Participant Deliverables:**
  1. Completed **Bid/No-Bid Decision Scorecard** justifying why the company will bid on Project Titan.
  2. Redlined **Site Survey Report** highlighting 6 critical site unknowns:
     - Unfinished drywall in the MDF room with missing 2-hour fire-rated plywood backboards.
     - 480V electrical switchgear running within 12 inches of planned low-voltage cable tray routes.
     - Unpaved, muddy trailer yard preventing scissor-lift access for perimeter camera mounting.
  3. Formal **Project Scope Statement** establishing explicit boundaries, deliverables, and mandatory Exclusionary Clauses:
     - *Exclusions:* 120V/208V AC electrical dedicated circuits, high-voltage conduit, core drilling through post-tension concrete, drywall patching/painting, and trenching in the exterior yard.

#### MILESTONE 2: PLANNING, CRITICAL PATH SCHEDULING, MARGIN & RISK
- **The Challenge:** Teams convert the scope into an executable operational plan.
- **Participant Deliverables:**
  1. Detailed **4-Level Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)** organizing work into 4 phases: Engineering & Staging, Rough-In & Pathways, Trim-Out & Head-End, Commissioning & Handover.
  2. **Critical Path Method (CPM) Schedule** mapped on a Gantt chart. Teams must recognize that the Cisco 9300 core switches have a 10-week factory lead time and the fire alarm voice evacuation panel has an 8-week engineering approval window from the local AHJ.
  3. **Comprehensive Cost & Margin Budget:** Pricing direct labor (1,420 technician hours at $52/hr burdened cost), hardware ($138,000 wholesale), equipment rentals ($8,400 for 3 scissor lifts), and risk contingency ($12,000), locking in a target Gross Margin of 36.5%.
  4. **Project Risk Register:** Identifying 8 high-consequence technical and operational risks with designated owners and preventive triggers.

#### MILESTONE 3: PROCUREMENT, PRE-STAGING & MOBILIZATION
- **The Challenge:** Teams execute procurement and prepare for mobilization.
- **Participant Deliverables:**
  1. **Supplier Comparison & Purchase Matrix:** Analyzing bids from three distributors, optimizing discounts, and establishing delivery milestones with 2-week buffer dates.
  2. **Pre-Staging Verification Protocol:** Formulating the shop testing process: Unboxing 52 cameras, assigning static IP addresses, burning in NVRs for 48 hours, updating switch firmware to enterprise release, and labeling all hardware before loading into job trailers.
  3. **Jobsite Kickoff Alignment Deck & Agenda:** Conducting the simulated Kickoff Meeting with the General Contractor Superintendent, Facility Director, and Electrical Subcontractor to lock down trade pathways, shared lift usage, and work hours.

During simulated Week 5 of installation, the facilitator unleashes three simultaneous field crises:
- **Inject 1 (Supply Chain Crisis):** The distributor announces that the 8 Cisco core switches are detained at an overseas port; delivery is delayed by 4 weeks. The scheduled network cutover is in 3 weeks.
- **Inject 2 (Client Scope Creep):** The Warehouse Logistics VP visits the site and demands 8 additional 4K cameras along the high-value electronics aisle and card-reader maglocks on two emergency exit doors. He states: *"Just get them installed; we'll figure out the billing at the end of the job."*
- **Inject 3 (Jobsite Safety Emergency):** A subcontractor apprentice pulling cable drops an aluminum fish tape across an energized 277V lighting junction box, creating an arc flash. The apprentice suffers flash burns, and the GC Safety Director issues an immediate site-wide Stop-Work Order for all low-voltage personnel.

1. *Triage the Safety Stop-Work:* Conduct emergency safety investigation, file incident report, implement mandatory safety retraining, and negotiate lifting the stop-work order within 24 hours.
2. *Resolve the Switch Delay:* Formulate the **Loaner Switch Strategy**: Deploy temporary shop inventory switches to maintain cabling terminations and camera focusing, preventing project paralysis.
3. *Enforce the Scope Boundary:* Use the 4-sentence verbal script with the Logistics VP; produce a formal **Change Order Request (COR #01)** pricing the 8 cameras and maglocks at $14,800 with a 5-day schedule extension, securing written authorization before pulling a single extra foot of wire.

### TEMPLATE 2: BID / NO-BID DECISION SCORECARD
- **Purpose:** A quantitative 10-metric scorecard preventing the company from bidding on catastrophic, low-margin, or high-liability jobs.
- **When Used:** Phase 0, before spending more than 1 hour on system engineering or pricing.
- **Who Completes It:** Estimator and Company Owner jointly.
- **Required Fields:** 10 Scoring Categories (1-10 points each): Client Credit/Payment History, Scope Clarity, Realistic Schedule, In-House Technical Capability, Equipment Availability, Margin Potential, Relationship/Competition, Liability/Liquidated Damages, Subcontractor Dependency, Site Accessibility. Threshold: <60 = No-Bid; 60-74 = Conditional Bid; 75-100 = Must Bid.
- **Realistic Filled-in Example:**
  ```text
  [BID / NO-BID QUANTITATIVE SCORECARD]
  Project: Metro Transit Maintenance Depot CCTV & Perimeter Security | Date: 2026-10-04
  Criteria & Scoring (Scale 1-10):
  1. Scope Clarity & Specifications: 3/10 (Vague "complete coverage" language, no wire runs shown).
  2. Realistic Project Timeline: 4/10 (Demands completion in 3 weeks; long-lead cameras take 6 weeks).
  3. Client Credit & Payment Terms: 8/10 (Municipal agency, pays reliably Net-45).
  4. Core Competency Fit: 9/10 (Enterprise VMS and fiber pulls are our core strength).
  5. Margin Potential: 4/10 (Public open low-bid procurement, race to the bottom).

  9. Subcontractor Reliance: 3/10 (Requires heavy asphalt trenching sub we do not control).
  10. Resource Availability: 6/10 (Lead technicians currently committed to hospital job).
  TOTAL SCORE: 48 / 100
  ```

modules.goal: Phase Goal: Send every person home intact. Ensure every high-risk task is permitted, every energized/hot-work/height task is isolated, and every worker holds personal stop-work authority — while treating a safety event as the schedule and financial event it actually is.
modules.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Risk Management, Project Resource Management, Project Quality Management.
concepts: The Permit-to-Work Gate: Six tasks in this trade never start without a signed permit and a Job Hazard Analysis (JHA): energized electrical work; hot work (soldering, brazing, grinding); working at heights above 2 m / 6 ft; ceiling and core drilling in occupied or healthcare spaces; confined-space entries (manholes, cable vaults, raised-floor plenums); and isolation of any life-safety device or fire alarm zone.

Lockout/Tagout Is Not the Electrician's Problem: Low-voltage contractors isolate and lock out the circuits they touch, verify absence of voltage themselves, and never trust a label. "The electrical sub said it was dead" is not a defense in an investigation.

Stop-Work Authority Is a Real Power — and a Real Obligation: Any worker, any trade, any day may stop a job for a safety reason with zero blame and zero financial consequence. The cost of a two-hour stop is trivial against a twenty-year injury. Management must say this out loud in week one, or it does not exist.

A Safety Incident Is a Project Management Event: An incident triggers a stop-work order, an investigation, possible authority involvement, insurance impact, and schedule slippage — frequently with liquidated damages still running. The risk register and schedule must carry that exposure, and the recovery plan must be written the same day.
Near-Misses Are Free Lessons: A near-miss reported today is the incident prevented tomorrow. Reporting must be blameless, one page, and acted on within 48 hours.

modules.title: CONTRACT RISK, COMPLIANCE, PRIVACY & CYBER-HARDENING
modules.phase: Lifecycle Phase: Cross-cutting — bid stage (contract risk), execution (permits and authority approvals), handover (privacy and cyber-hardening)
modules.goal: Phase Goal: Stop signing unlimited liability, deliver systems that are lawful to operate and defensible in court, and hand over networked security systems that are not the weakest link in the client's network.
modules.pmbok: PMBOK Alignment: Project Procurement Management (Contract Types), Project Risk Management, Stakeholder Engagement.
concepts: The Five Contract Traps: Uncapped indemnity; consequential damages not excluded; liquidated damages with no excusable-delay clause; "pay-when-paid" flow-down from a GC; and insurance/COI requirements you cannot actually meet. Every one is negotiable before signature and a lawsuit after.

Compliance Is a Schedule Item, Not a Formality: Permits, authority (AHJ) approval windows, engineering submittals for listed systems, and licensing/certification requirements have lead times measured in weeks. If they are not on the critical path, the schedule is fiction.

A Camera System Is a Data-Processing System: Surveillance triggers data-protection obligations in most jurisdictions: signage in monitored zones, a defined lawful basis, a retention clock (30/90 days — never "until the disk is full"), access limited to need-to-know, secure storage, an audit trail for every export, a defined response path for data-subject requests, and — in many regions — registration with the data-protection authority. Placement is restricted (never in restrooms, changing rooms, or private spaces), and audio recording usually requires its own legal basis.

Footage Without a Timestamp Is Not Evidence: Time synchronization (NTP), chain of custody, and access logs decide whether recordings are admissible. Cyber-hardening is therefore part of system quality, not an optional extra.

You Are Installing the Client's Most Hackable Asset: Cameras, NVRs, and access controllers left on default credentials, exposed management ports, and outdated firmware are the entry point ransomware uses to encrypt a business. Delivering them in that state is a defect, not a feature.

sequence.example: Technical Example: Handing over a 60-camera city-center CCTV and access-control system for a retail client.
sequence.problem: Business Problem: The contract carried an uncapped indemnity and made the contractor "responsible for the lawful operation of the recording system"; cameras still ran default passwords; the NVR was reachable on a public management port; recordings had no set retention; and no signage informed the public. The client's counsel demands a data-protection statement, a subject-access request is filed, and ransomware enters the client's network through the NVR six months later.

sequence.application: Field Application: Every proposal carries the limitation-of-liability and exclusion clause set; every security installation is delivered with a signed privacy sheet and hardening certificate; no system ships on default credentials.

## WORKSHOP 1: BID/NO-BID & SCOPE DISCOVERY ON A VAGUE SECURITY-INTEGRATION RFP
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 0 — Pre-Sales / Opportunity Qualification
- **Business Line:** Physical Security System Integration (CCTV + Access Control + Intrusion)
- **Realistic Scenario:** A regional property management group issues a 4-page RFP for "Turnkey Security Modernization" across a 5-building commercial office park. The RFP states: *"Provide complete CCTV coverage of all parking lots and building perimeters, card access on all perimeter doors, intrusion detection, and connection to a central monitoring station. Bid must be fixed-price lump-sum. Proposal due in 5 business days. Project must be complete in 6 weeks. 10% retention withheld for 12 months."* No drawings, no drop counts, no camera specs, and no cable pathway data are provided.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):** 
  1. Evaluate an ambiguous RFP using a quantitative 10-criteria Bid/No-Bid Scorecard.
  2. Draft a targeted Pre-Bid Clarification Request that flushes out technical and financial traps without alienating the client.
  3. Formulate an exclusionary scope boundary statement defending the contractor against unlimited liability.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 0 (Pre-Sales & Opportunity Qualification).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 90 Minutes (15m Scenario Briefing & RFP Review, 40m Team Analysis & Tool Execution, 25m Cross-Team Defense & Debrief, 10m Monday-Morning Habit Transfer).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Company Owner / Sales Director* (wants the revenue, tempted to bid blind).
  - *Role B: Estimator / Senior PM* (calculates risk, identifies missing engineering data).
  - *Role C: Lead Field Technician* (evaluates physical reality: mounting heights, trenching, power).
  - *Role D: Client Representative / GC* (defends the vague RFP, presses for a cheap number).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Copy of the 4-page ambiguous RFP and sample standard GC subcontractor agreement with indemnity clauses.
  - Historical win/loss data showing margin erosion on similar "turnkey" RFPs.
- **The Task:**
  1. Score the RFP using the Bid/No-Bid Decision Scorecard.
  2. If score is below 70, formulate the exact Go/No-Go recommendation and conditions.
  3. Draft 5 mandatory Technical Clarification Questions for the client.
  4. Write a 1-paragraph Scope Assumption Statement to accompany any preliminary budgetary estimate.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Completed Bid/No-Bid Scorecard, Technical Clarification Letter, and Preliminary Scope Boundary Log.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "Notice the clause 'turnkey security modernization.' If the parking lot requires directional boring and conduit trenching 400 feet under asphalt, who pays for it under this wording?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* Help learners realize that submitting a lump-sum price on a vague RFP is not selling; it is gambling with company equity.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Assuming the client will be "reasonable" later when unforeseen costs emerge. *Debrief:* Show that in fixed-price contracting, ambiguity legally favors the buyer unless explicitly excluded.
  2. *Mistake:* Spending 20 hours designing a system without knowing if the client has a realistic budget. *Debrief:* Establish the rule of the "Qualifying Phone Call" to establish budget ranges before detailed engineering.
  3. *Mistake:* Failing to identify civil work (trenching, conduit, core drilling, 120V power). *Debrief:* Teach the standard low-voltage exclusion clause: *"All conduit, pathway, coring, and 120VAC power provided by others."*
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Recommends bidding blind lump-sum; misses trenching and pathway risks.
  - *2 (Developing):* Identifies missing specs but fails to attach contractual assumptions to the bid.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Scores RFP objectively; writes clear pre-bid questions and standard trade exclusions.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Successfully negotiates a paid engineering/site-survey phase with the client before bidding.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Put the 1-Page Bid/No-Bid Scorecard on the estimator's desk. Any RFP scoring below 65 is either rejected or converted into a paid discovery walk.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Owner runs the scorecard solo in 10 minutes to protect limited technician time.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Estimator and Lead PM review the scorecard jointly before proposal kickoff.

## WORKSHOP 2: STAKEHOLDER MAPPING & SITE WALK FOR A FIRE ALARM REPLACEMENT IN AN OCCUPIED HEALTHCARE WING
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 1 — Project Initiation & Site Survey
- **Business Line:** Fire Alarm & Life-Safety Systems
- **Realistic Scenario:** A 40-bed specialized sub-acute healthcare facility requires the replacement of an obsolete legacy conventional fire alarm panel with a new addressable voice-evacuation system (Notifier NFS2-3030 with voice). The facility is 100% occupied with high-dependency patients, immunocompromised wards, and locked memory-care units. Ceiling spaces are known to contain asbestos-containing insulation in older wings. Work must not trigger false alarms or disrupt patient care.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Construct a comprehensive Stakeholder Register and Communication Protocol for a high-consequence healthcare environment.
  2. Conduct a simulated multi-dimensional Site Walk identifying infection control (ICRA), asbestos, and ceiling access barriers.
  3. Formulate an Infection Control & Life-Safety Phased Cutover Plan maintaining active detection 24/7.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 1 (Initiation & Site Survey).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 120 Minutes (20m Scenario Briefing & Healthcare Regulations, 50m Site Survey Simulation & Redlining, 35m Stakeholder Strategy Presentation, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 4 to 5 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Healthcare Facility Director* (hyper-focused on patient safety, zero false alarms, noise control).
  - *Role B: Infection Control Officer (ICRA)* (demands containment tents, HEPA vacuums, negative air pressure).
  - *Role C: Contractor Lead Fire Alarm PM* (responsible for schedule, budget, and system functionality).
  - *Role D: Field Lead Technician / Electrician* (responsible for physical wire pulls, ladder placement, device replacement).
  - *Role E: Local Fire Marshal / AHJ* (demands uninterrupted life-safety coverage during construction).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Architectural floor plan of the healthcare wing showing patient rooms, nurses' stations, and fire barriers.
  - Existing legacy fire alarm single-line drawing (incomplete).
  - Hospital Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA) Class IV protocol sheet.
- **The Task:**
  1. Map all internal and external stakeholders with their authority level, primary fears, and communication needs.
  2. Complete the Healthcare Site Walk Checklist identifying 8 hidden operational constraints.
  3. Create an Interim Life Safety Measures (ILSM) cutover schedule guaranteeing continuous fire alarm protection.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Healthcare Stakeholder Matrix, Completed Site Walk Hazard Log, and ILSM Operational Phasing Plan.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "If your technician drills into a ceiling tile in Ward B without an ICRA containment tent, what happens? Who can shut down your job site in 30 seconds?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* In life-safety and healthcare, technical installation is only 30% of the job; stakeholder and environmental compliance is 70%.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Treating a hospital like a standard commercial office; drilling ceilings without containment. *Debrief:* Explain ICRA Class IV fines, shut-downs, and health risks.
  2. *Mistake:* Failing to coordinate with the local Fire Department before taking a legacy zone offline. *Debrief:* Demonstrate the mandatory Fire Watch procedure and AHJ notification protocols.
  3. *Mistake:* Forgetting patient rest hours and acoustic restrictions. *Debrief:* Show how labor estimates must account for off-hours, noisy-work windows (6:00 AM - 8:00 AM only).
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Ignores ICRA requirements; plans daytime strobe testing in active patient rooms.
  - *2 (Developing):* Recognizes asbestos and ICRA but fails to account for 24/7 fire watch labor costs.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Comprehensive stakeholder map; includes mobile dust containment and phased zone cutovers.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Delivers a turn-key ILSM manual that the hospital safety committee approves without edits.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Before stepping foot on any occupied commercial, industrial, or healthcare site, complete the Pre-Walk Stakeholder Checklist and identify the site authority who controls work permits.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Focus heavily on the practical daily cost of off-hours labor and containment equipment rental.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Establish formal role separation between the Safety Coordinator and Project Manager.

## WORKSHOP 3: WBS DECOMPOSITION FOR A MULTI-SITE CCTV & ACCESS CONTROL ROLLOUT ACROSS 12 RETAIL BRANCHES
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 2 — Planning
- **Business Line:** Video Surveillance & Access Control
- **Realistic Scenario:** A regional credit union awards your company a contract to deploy an integrated IP video and access control solution across 12 branch locations spread over a 150-mile radius. Each branch requires: 8 IP cameras (Hanwha 4K), 1 8-channel NVR with cloud sync, 3 card access doors (Software House iSTAR Edge), intercom integration at the drive-through, and local panic button tie-ins. All branches must remain fully operational during business hours. Work must be finished in 60 calendar days.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Decompose a multi-site technical integration project into a 4-level Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) with 100% rule compliance.
  2. Define measurable Work Packages with distinct completion criteria, labor budgets, and responsible roles.
  3. Standardize branch rollout packages to create a repeatable "cookie-cutter" operational template.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 2 (WBS, Schedule & Cost Planning).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 105 Minutes (15m WBS Theory & Multi-Site Pitfalls, 45m Team WBS Decomposition, 30m Cross-Team Review & Gap Analysis, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Senior Project Manager* (governs multi-site schedule, standardization, and branch reporting).
  - *Role B: Field Lead Foreman* (manages physical travel, rough-in, device mounting, and branch technicians).
  - *Role C: Systems Integration Programmer* (handles NVR pre-staging, IP addressing, VMS cloud enrollment, reader programming).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Branch archetype floor plan (standard retail banking layout: teller line, vault, ATM lobby, manager office, drive-through).
  - Scope overview document detailing hardware quantities and milestone deadlines.
- **The Task:**
  1. Build a graphical or indented 4-level WBS covering all phases (Central Engineering/Staging -> Branch Deployment -> Branch Commissioning -> Program Closeout).
  2. Create a WBS Dictionary entry for two critical work packages: *WP 2.3: Branch Staged Pre-Configuration* and *WP 3.4: Branch Physical Cutover & Acceptance*.
  3. Define the exact "Done" criteria for a branch to prevent technicians from leaving unfinished punch items behind.
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** Complete Multi-Site Rollout WBS Tree, WBS Dictionary Cards for key work packages.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "If your team travels 2 hours to Branch 7 and realizes the network switches haven't been configured by the bank's IT department, where did your WBS fail?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* The 100% Rule—if an activity (such as travel time, van restocking, or customer network coordination) is not in the WBS, it is not in the budget.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Structuring the WBS by physical trade tasks only, ignoring central procurement, staging, and administrative closeout. *Debrief:* Show that staging in the shop saves 60% of field travel time.
  2. *Mistake:* Vague work package definitions (e.g., "Install Cameras" instead of "Mount, Terminate, Aim, Focus, and Capture Acceptance Snapshot"). *Debrief:* Vague definitions lead to infinite punch lists.
  3. *Mistake:* Neglecting multi-site mobilization logistics (drive time, per diem, vehicle maintenance). *Debrief:* Factor travel and logistics directly into the WBS as distinct work packages.
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Merely lists hardware components without chronological or logical work packages.
  - *2 (Developing):* Captures physical site work but misses pre-staging, travel logistics, and client IT coordination.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Well-structured 4-level WBS with clear work packages, dictionary definitions, and measurable completion gates.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Produces a highly optimized, modular "cookie-cutter" WBS where any technician can execute an identical branch deployment without supervision.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Never start a multi-location job without a standardized WBS template that includes Shop Staging, Field Deployment, and Client Sign-Off gates.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Consolidate WBS to 3 levels; combine staging and procurement into a single lead technician package.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Assign dedicated package owners (Central Staging Engineer vs. Mobile Field Foreman).

## WORKSHOP 4: CPM SCHEDULING & RESOURCE LEVELING WITH A 2-TECH CREW & LONG EQUIPMENT LEAD TIMES
- **Lifecycle Phase:** Phase 2 — Planning
- **Business Line:** Computer Networks & Structured Cabling
- **Realistic Scenario:** A distribution logistics company is expanding into a new 80,000 sq ft warehouse. The scope includes: 140 Cat6A network drops, 12 industrial wireless access points (Aruba AP-555), 2 IDF wall-mount server cabinets, and a fiber optic 10G backbone link to the main office MDF (500-foot armored multi-mode fiber pull with fusion splicing). 
  - *Resources Available:* Only 2 full-time technicians (Lead Tech Dave, Junior Tech Sam).
  - *Constraints:* The industrial PoE switches and specialized fiber patch panels have a strict 10-week factory lead time. The warehouse racking installation starts in Week 4. The concrete floor polishing starts in Week 6 (no lifts allowed on floor for 10 days). Customer occupancy date is fixed at Week 12.
- **Learning Objectives (Observable):**
  1. Construct a Critical Path Method (CPM) network diagram calculating Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Float.
  2. Identify the true Critical Path driving the project delivery date under long procurement lead times.
  3. Perform Resource Leveling for a 2-person crew to eliminate over-allocation while respecting site access blackouts.
- **Prerequisite Module:** Module 2 (WBS, Schedule & Cost Planning).
- **Duration & Pacing:** 120 Minutes (20m Critical Path & Lead Time Mechanics, 50m Scheduling & Leveling Exercise, 35m Schedule Optimization Defense, 15m Debrief).
- **Group Size & Roles:** 3 to 4 participants per team:
  - *Role A: Project Scheduler / Operations Manager* (balances company-wide crew allocations).
  - *Role B: Lead Field Technician* (understands daily wire-pull productivity and scissor-lift constraints).
  - *Role C: General Contractor Representative* (defends the floor polishing and racking dates; refuses schedule slips).
- **Inputs & Artifacts Provided:**
  - Activity list with estimated durations (in tech-hours) and strict physical dependencies.
  - Calendar constraint sheet (concrete floor curing window, scissor lift rental dates, equipment ship dates).
- **The Task:**
  1. Build a sequenced CPM schedule identifying Total Float for all non-critical paths.
  2. Map out the 2-technician daily allocation across the 12-week timeline.
  3. Resolve the resource clash: Day 18 through Day 24 requires 3 technicians to beat the floor polisher deadline. Propose a viable contractor solution (overtime, phased pull, or pre-pulling fiber pathways).
- **Expected Deliverables Produced:** CPM Network Logic Chart, Resource-Leveled Gantt Schedule, and Lead-Time Risk Mitigation Plan.
- **Facilitator Guide & Guiding Prompts:**
  - *Prompt:* "Look at Week 1. Dave and Sam are scheduled to pull cable, but the scissor lifts haven't arrived and the unistrut isn't installed. If you start pulling wire on the floor, what happens to productivity?"
  - *Teaching Moment:* Lead times are not passive waiting periods; they are active critical path items that require milestone tracking just like physical installation.
- **3 Most Common Field Mistakes & Debrief:**
  1. *Mistake:* Scheduling installation assuming equipment is magically on site on Day 1. *Debrief:* Show how ordering equipment without tracking PO confirmation dates triggers crew idle time.
  2. *Mistake:* Over-allocating the lead tech to 60 hours in a week without factoring fatigue, rework, or vehicle travel. *Debrief:* Demonstrate sustainable 35-billable-hour scheduling models for small crews.
  3. *Mistake:* Ignoring other trades' hard site constraints (e.g., polished concrete curing). *Debrief:* Emphasize coordinating high-reach work before floor treatments or racking obstructs aerial access.
- **Assessment Rubric (1 to 4 Scale):**
  - *1 (Deficient):* Ignores the 10-week equipment lead time; creates an unexecutable schedule with massive resource clashes.
  - *2 (Developing):* Identifies lead times but fails to level technician hours; overlaps work during the concrete cure window.
  - *3 (Proficient):* Accurate CPM diagram; correctly identifies critical path; levels 2-tech crew around site blackouts.
  - *4 (Exemplary):* Optimizes the schedule by pre-pulling home-runs during empty warehouse windows, saving 15% in lift rental costs.
- **So What Monday Morning Transfer:** Whenever a quote contains equipment with a lead time exceeding 3 weeks, place an "Equipment PO Placed & Confirmed" milestone at the top of the job schedule.
- **Variations (5-Person vs. 30-Person SME):**
  - *5-Person Shop:* Focus heavily on the cash impact of rental lifts sitting idle while waiting for cable.
  - *30-Person Firm:* Cross-level technicians between two different commercial projects to absorb float.

### TEMPLATE 2: BID / NO-BID DECISION SCORECARD
- **Purpose:** A quantitative 10-metric scorecard preventing the company from bidding on catastrophic, low-margin, or high-liability jobs.
- **When Used:** Phase 0, before spending more than 1 hour on system engineering or pricing.
- **Who Completes It:** Estimator and Company Owner jointly.
- **Required Fields:** 10 Scoring Categories (1-10 points each): Client Credit/Payment History, Scope Clarity, Realistic Schedule, In-House Technical Capability, Equipment Availability, Margin Potential, Relationship/Competition, Liability/Liquidated Damages, Subcontractor Dependency, Site Accessibility. Threshold: <60 = No-Bid; 60-74 = Conditional Bid; 75-100 = Must Bid.
- **Realistic Filled-in Example:**
  ```text
  [BID / NO-BID QUANTITATIVE SCORECARD]
  Project: Metro Transit Maintenance Depot CCTV & Perimeter Security | Date: 2026-10-04
  Criteria & Scoring (Scale 1-10):
  1. Scope Clarity & Specifications: 3/10 (Vague "complete coverage" language, no wire runs shown).
  2. Realistic Project Timeline: 4/10 (Demands completion in 3 weeks; long-lead cameras take 6 weeks).
  3. Client Credit & Payment Terms: 8/10 (Municipal agency, pays reliably Net-45).
  4. Core Competency Fit: 9/10 (Enterprise VMS and fiber pulls are our core strength).
  5. Margin Potential: 4/10 (Public open low-bid procurement, race to the bottom).
  6. Competitive Position: 5/10 (8 competing bidders expected).
  7. Risk & Liquidated Damages: 2/10 (Severe $1,500/day penalty clause for delays).
  8. Material & Supply Chain Risk: 4/10 (Outdoor PTZ poles and trenching required).
  9. Subcontractor Reliance: 3/10 (Requires heavy asphalt trenching sub we do not control).
  10. Resource Availability: 6/10 (Lead technicians currently committed to hospital job).
  TOTAL SCORE: 48 / 100
  DECISION: STRICT NO-BID. (Reason: Severe liquidated damages + 3-week timeline + long-lead hardware).
  ```

```
### 8.32 TEMPLATE ADOPTION SEQUENCE — DEPLOY IN THIS ORDER
No SME adopts 31 templates at once. This is the proven rollout order, staged so each week's tools pay for the next week's training time:

| Week | Templates to Deploy | What It Stops |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Week 1** | Project Intake Form · Bid/No-Bid Scorecard · Scope Statement (incl. exclusions) | Bidding bad jobs; quoting without a scope; the biggest money leak. |

| **Week 3** | Delivery Tracking Register · Field Change Order Form · Daily Site Report | Partial/late deliveries; unbilled extras; "he said / she said" disputes. |

> **Rule:** Weeks 1–5 are the non-negotiable core. A company that deploys only those five weeks still captures roughly 80% of the program's financial benefit. The Week 6+ tools are for firms that have already proven the habit.
```

kpis.trigger: > 5.0%: Retrain crew on termination & pathway standards.

kpis.name: BOM Lead-Time Variance
kpis.formula: `Promised Distributor Ship Date - Actual Shop Receipt Date`
kpis.trigger: Lead time slip > 3 days: Re-route order or deploy loaners.

kpis.name: Unresolved Field Blockers
kpis.formula: `Number of Active Site Issues Open > 48 Hours`
kpis.trigger: Any blocker > 48h: Escalate directly to Company Owner.

kpis.name: Technician Billable Utilization
kpis.formula: `(Direct Billable Job Hours / Total Paid Hours) * 100`
kpis.trigger: < 75%: Too much unbilled shop travel or missing material runs.

kpis.name: Closeout Dossier Turnaround
kpis.formula: `Days from Commissioning to Complete O&M Package Delivery`
kpis.trigger: > 10 Days: Pre-build as-built drawings during trim-out phase.

cards.title: THE 5 QUESTIONS BEFORE TOUCHING A WIRE                                   │
lines: 1. Is this device and location explicitly listed in the contract Scope Statement?
2. Is there approved, dry pathway (conduit/J-hooks) separated from high voltage?
3. Is 120V AC electrical power and clean grounding verified in the rack room?
4. Has the client provided confirmed static IP addresses and switch port assignments?
5. If this is extra work, do I have a signed Change Order or written PM authorization?
RULE: IF YOU ANSWER "NO" TO ANY QUESTION, STOP AND CALL THE PROJECT MANAGER.

cards.title: THE 4-SENTENCE CHANGE SCRIPT (CAN YOU JUST...)                           │
lines: 1. "We can absolutely take care of that for you, no problem." (Positive Validation)
2. "That specific work is outside our contracted baseline scope." (Clear Boundary)
3. "Let me document the exact requirements so our PM can get you a price today."
4. "As soon as you sign off on that quick addendum, our crew will pull the wire."
RULE: NEVER ARGUE. NEVER DO IT FOR FREE. NEVER SAY "NO." PIVOT TO A PAID CHANGE ORDER.

cards.title: THE DAILY 5-MINUTE SITE STANDUP ROUTINE                                   │
lines: 1. WHAT ARE WE FINISHING TODAY? (Exact physical drops, devices, terminations).
2. WHAT TOOLS / MATERIALS ARE MISSING? (Check before 07:30 AM, not at 2:00 PM).
3. WHAT SITE HAZARDS ARE ACTIVE? (Ladders, scissor lifts, electrical panels, drywall).
4. WHO DO WE NEED TO COORDINATE WITH? (GC Super, electrician, client IT lead).
5. ARE THERE ANY POTENTIAL EXTRAS? (Log any client requests on the Daily Site Report).

cards.title: THE 10-POINT PRE-AHJ INSPECTION CHECKLIST                                │
lines: [ ] 1. Approved, stamped plans and permit placard posted at panel.
[ ] 2. Battery standby and voltage-drop calculations in binder.
[ ] 3. 100% of initiating devices pre-tested (smoke, heat, duct, pull stations).
[ ] 4. Strobe synchronization verified across all visible corridors.
[ ] 5. HVAC duct detectors shut down air handlers within 3 seconds.
[ ] 6. Magnetic door holders release and latches close fully on alarm.
[ ] 7. Access control stairwell doors drop to fail-safe unlocked instantly.
[ ] 8. Primary and secondary elevator recall floors operate correctly.
[ ] 9. Central monitoring station receiving alarm, supervisory, and trouble signals.
[ ] 10. Clean 120V breaker lockout installed and labeled in red.

cards.title: THE ZERO-DEFECT HANDOVER DOSSIER (RETENTION ACCELERATOR)                 │
lines: 1. Certificate of Substantial Completion (Signed by Client Executive).
2. Punch List Clearance Sheet (All items cleared within 72 hours).
3. As-Built Redline Drawings (Clean PDF showing exact device locations & cable routes).
4. Cable Certification Test Results (100% Pass Fluke PDF report).
5. Master IP / VLAN / MAC Address & Password Credentials Table.
6. Manufacturer Equipment Warranty Certificates & O&M Manuals.
7. Client Training Attendance Sign-Off Sheet.
8. Annual Maintenance SLA Agreement Proposal (Attached to final billing).

cards.title: SAFETY STOP-WORK AUTHORITY & PERMIT GATES                                 │
lines: WORK THAT NEEDS A SIGNED PERMIT + JOB HAZARD ANALYSIS BEFORE YOU START:
1. Energized electrical work, or any circuit you must touch.
2. Hot work: soldering, brazing, grinding, open flame.
3. Work above 2 m / 6 ft: ladders, lifts, scaffolds.
4. Core drilling or ceiling work in occupied or healthcare spaces.
5. Confined space: manholes, vaults, raised floors, cable trenches.
6. Isolating any life-safety device or fire alarm zone.
STOP-WORK RULE: If it feels wrong, STOP. Anyone may stop. No blame, no cost to you.
A two-hour stop beats a twenty-year injury.
AFTER ANY INCIDENT (THE FIRST 30 MINUTES):
1. Make the area safe. Isolate. Headcount.
2. First aid. Call emergency services if needed.
3. Notify your PM and the company owner immediately.
4. Do NOT clean up or move equipment — preserve the scene.
5. Write the 1-page incident report the same day.
RULE: "IT'S DEAD" IS NOT A TEST. LOCK IT, VERIFY IT, OR DON'T TOUCH IT.

cards.title: CYBER-HARDENING AT HANDOVER (10 CHECKS)                                   │
lines: 1. Default credentials changed — unique per device, stored in a password manager.
2. Cameras, NVRs, controllers on a dedicated VLAN, isolated from client data.
3. Firmware current on every device before delivery.
4. NTP time sync working — timestamps are what make footage evidence.
5. Unused services off; public management ports closed; remote access via VPN only.
6. Management over HTTPS/SSH only — no plain-text protocols.
7. Logging enabled, with defined retention and protected log storage.
8. Configurations backed up and restorable; backups tested once.
9. Recording retention set explicitly (30/90 days) and overwrite verified.
10. Credentials handed over with a signed receipt; client trained to change them.
RULE: A SECURITY SYSTEM YOU CAN'T HARDEN IS A DEFECT, NOT A DELIVERY.

cards.title: PRIVACY & DATA PROTECTION FOR SECURITY INSTALLATIONS                      │
lines: 1. SIGNS: Clear signage at every monitored entrance and zone — purpose + controller.
2. LAWFUL BASIS: Document why recording is needed and who the data controller is.
3. RETENTION: Set an explicit clock (30/90 days). "Until the disk is full" is not one.
4. NEVER HERE: No cameras in restrooms, changing rooms, break rooms. Check sightlines.
5. ACCESS: Need-to-know only, named operators, unique logins, no shared admin account.
6. AUDIT TRAIL: Every export logged — who, what, when, why.
7. SUBJECT REQUESTS: A defined path and a 30-day response for "show me my footage."
8. AUDIO: Usually needs its own legal basis — record only with written authority.
9. STORAGE: Encrypted at rest where supported; NVR in a locked, access-controlled room.
10. DOCUMENT IT: Signed privacy sheet at handover — your advice and the client's choices
on the record.
RULE: IF YOU CAN'T SHOW THE POLICY, YOU CAN'T DEFEND THE FOOTAGE.
